I will keep to the cropping pattern I trust most here in Quzhou County: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. That is the steadiest way for me to use a full year, spread risk, and make use of the local weather, irrigation habits, and the machinery and inputs I already understand. At my age and with my experience, I do not want to gamble on crops that need more market timing or more delicate field management. Wheat and maize are familiar, the sales are straightforward, and I know how to manage fertilizer, water, weeds, and pests without making the year too uncertain.

For seed, I will use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed, because I care more about stable yield and resistance than saving a little money on seed. For tillage, I will use rotary tillage before wheat so I can prepare a clean seedbed after the summer crop, and I will use no-tillage direct seeding for maize after wheat harvest to save time and hold moisture. I will not push fertilizer too hard, because too much nitrogen can make wheat lodge and can waste money; I will feed enough for steady yield. I will irrigate wheat more than maize because wheat here depends more on timely spring water, while maize can catch summer rain if the season is normal. I will keep pesticide use moderate, applying only enough times to control the usual diseases, insects, and weeds that threaten yield.
